findings.title: Tagging a run with a Delegate=yes systemd scope switches on the cpu controller for every sibling app group and changes how the user's CPU is shared (fixed rule 1)
findings.evidence: Probe a-linux/cgroup_side_effects.out.txt: 'Delegate=yes: scope has [cpu memory pids]; app.slice passes down [cpu memory pids] while it runs; ... cpu.weight True'; 'Delegate=memory pids: ... app.slice passes down [memory pids]'; 'cpu controller not passed down to X and Y: X gets 20%' / 'passed down: X gets 50%'. Re-read now (verify-4/linux_platform_readonly.out.txt): app.slice passes down 'memory pids'; 22 groups directly below app.slice; user@N.service DelegateControllers=cpu memory pids. systemd 255 man page and https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.resource-control.html (re-fetched): Delegate=yes means 'all supported controllers are enabled for the unit'; '...any controllers that are delegated will be enabled for the parent and sibling units of the unit with delegation'; units with a controller enabled 'may be subject to resource control even if they do not have any explicit configuration'. https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html (re-fetched) on cpu.stat: 'This file exists whether the controller is enabled or not.' Brief: docs/17-build-prompt.md:23 allows cgroup placement and forbids only limits; :42 sends the builder to 'cgroup v2 delegation' docs; :69 'Set no limits'. Nothing names which controllers.
findings.impact: While any tagged run is live, the 22 sibling app groups switch from per-thread to per-group CPU sharing (one busy process in X against four in Y: 20% becomes 50%). That changes the scheduling of processes Submeter did not launch, which fixed rule 1 forbids, and it changes the tagged run's own CPU share, i.e. the figure being measured. It also exposes cpu.weight/cpu.max on those groups, 'a setting that enables' a priority change. The run's accounting needs none of it: cpu.stat exists without the cpu controller.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md after line 69: 'On Linux, delegate to the run's scope only controllers its parent slice already passes down (read the parent's cgroup.subtree_control first), normally memory and pids. Never enable the cpu or io controller anywhere and never write cpu.weight or cpu.max: enabling a controller turns it on for every sibling group, and cpu.stat is present without it.' docs/09-telemetry.md row 1, Linux column: 'cgroup v2: cpu.stat always (no cpu controller needed); memory and pids files when the parent slice passes them down'.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/17:23,42,62,69 and grepped docs/ for cgroup/delegat/systemd/cpu.weight: no controller guidance anywhere, so not handled; no R-number covers it. Did NOT re-run the probe: both parts would themselves enable cpu on app.slice or burn a CPU and so disturb the other verifiers' timing. Instead re-checked the state read-only with my own probe (app.slice 'memory pids', 22 siblings, user@ delegates cpu memory pids, no probe cgroups left) and confirmed the mechanism in the local systemd 255 man page and the re-fetched freedesktop and kernel pages (quotes above). The 20%/50% split matches per-thread vs per-group fairness exactly, which the man page's example also describes ('the cpu controller would not be enabled for units in those slices and CPU resources would be further allocated using other mechanisms, e.g. based on nice levels'). Severity kept critical: the brief authorises cgroup placement, points the builder at delegation docs whose default is Delegate=yes, and only forbids limits, so the natural build breaks rule 1. Changed the proposal from a fixed 'memory pids' list to 'only what the parent already passes down', because on a distro whose app.slice does not pass memory down, Delegate=memory would also enable memory on every sibling.

findings.title: The brief never says where a Linux tagged cgroup lives; the only unprivileged, systemd-sanctioned place is a delegated transient user scope with holder and payload leaf groups, and R15 misstates cgroup removal
findings.evidence: verify-4/linux_platform_readonly.out.txt: user.slice and user-N.slice owner uid 0, cgroup.procs uid 0; user@N.service owned by this user; this process's own group passes down 'nothing'. a-linux/cgroup_totals.out.txt A: group made below the shell's own cgroup 'cpu.stat yes, memory.current NO, memory.peak NO, pids.current NO'; 2: mkdir group 'directory still there: True; populated 0'. a-linux/cgroup_scope.out.txt 2: Delegate scope 'passing memory down while this process is in it: refused (Device or resource busy)', 'moving this process into a sub-group: allowed', payload memory.peak readable after last exit; 3: once empty 'scope directory, with the sub-groups made inside it, still there: False', 'LoadState=not-found'; 4: no session bus 'Failed to connect to bus: No medium found'. https://systemd.io/CGROUP_DELEGATION/ (re-fetched): 'Never create your own cgroups below arbitrary cgroups systemd manages, i.e cgroups you haven't set Delegate= in.'; 'it's not permitted to have processes directly attached to a cgroup that also has child cgroups'; suggested layout a 'supervisor/' leaf and 'payload-xyz/' leaves. Kernel cgroup-v2 doc (re-fetched): 'A cgroup which doesn't have any children or live processes can be destroyed by removing the directory.' docs/16-review-log.md:145 (R15): 'A cgroup is removed once it is empty.' docs/09:9 and docs/17:42 are the only Linux guidance.
findings.impact: Phase 2's gate ('final totals survive its exit', background processes still accounted) depends on a layout the brief leaves to guesswork. A group under the shell's own scope gives CPU only and breaks systemd's single-writer rule; a plain scope is deleted with its counters the moment it empties; mkdir groups leak a directory per crashed run. Under su, sudo -u, cron or a system service there is no user bus, so tagged runs cannot be created at all. R15's premise is true only for systemd scopes.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md, a Linux paragraph after line 62: 'On Linux, ask the signed-in user's systemd over the user bus for a transient scope with Delegate set to the controllers its slice already passes down (see the controller rule). Inside it make leaf groups: holder for the waiting process and payload for the command; payload passes its controllers down and runs the command in payload/main, so a nested run can make a sibling under payload with the same files. The holder watches payload/cgroup.events; when populated is 0 it reads cpu.stat, memory.peak, memory.stat and pids.peak, writes the run file and exits, and systemd removes the scope. Never make cgroups outside such a scope. With no user bus (su, sudo -u, cron, a system service, WSL without systemd), say that tagged runs are unavailable and run the command polled.' docs/16-review-log.md R15: 'systemd removes a scope once it is empty; a cgroup made with mkdir stays until it is removed.'
findings.cost: One paragraph in docs/17 and one corrected clause in R15.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/09:9, docs/17:42,62-69 and R15; grepped docs/ for cgroup/systemd/delegat: no placement, layout or no-bus rule anywhere, R15 covers only who reads final totals. Re-checked ownership and pass-down state read-only with my own probe (matches the lead's table). Did not re-run cgroup_scope.py or cgroup_totals.py: the first creates a Delegate=yes scope (which, per L1, changes sibling CPU sharing while other verifiers time things) and the second burns CPU. Re-fetched systemd.io and the kernel doc: both quotes are present and mean what the lead says; systemd.io's supervisor/payload layout matches the proposal. Amended the proposal to (a) take the Delegate list from L1 instead of hard-coding it and (b) run the command in payload/main so nested runs keep memory and pids (from cgroup_totals 6: a group nested under a pass-down group has memory.current and memory.peak; a pass-down group cannot hold processes). That layout is reasoned from the probe's rules, not run end to end. Unverified extra: Linux CI runners may lack a user bus too, which would block the phase 2 gate on CI.
findings.would_confirm: For the CI side note only: run 'systemd-run --user --scope true' in a GitHub Actions ubuntu job and see whether it fails with 'Failed to connect to bus'.

findings.title: On Linux a tagged group has no I/O totals and no count of processes started, though docs/17, docs/05 and docs/09 present both as authoritative and Full
findings.evidence: verify-4 probe: root passes down 'cpuset cpu io memory ...', user.slice passes down 'cpu memory pids' (no io from that level on); app.slice io.* files: ['io.pressure'] only; 'files that could count processes started: none'; pids files: pids.current, pids.events, pids.events.local, pids.max, pids.peak. /usr/lib/systemd/system/user@.service:24 'Delegate=pids memory cpu'. a-linux/cgroup_whole_machine.out.txt: delegated to this user 74 cgroups, 'io.stat present in 0'. cgroup_totals 3: '8 extra threads: pids.current 9, lines in cgroup.procs 1'. Kernel doc (re-fetched): 'Note that PIDs used in this controller refer to TIDs, process IDs as used by the kernel.' Windows has the counter: learn.microsoft.com JOBOBJECT_BASIC_ACCOUNTING_INFORMATION (re-fetched) TotalProcesses 'The total number of processes associated with the job during its lifetime, including those that have terminated.' Claims: docs/17-build-prompt.md:62 'authoritative: CPU time, memory, I/O and process counts'; docs/05-data-flow.md:52 'the kernel totals CPU, memory and I/O'; docs/09-telemetry.md:9 'Without admin: Full'; docs/17:127 run totals include 'I/O, processes started'.
findings.impact: Linux tagged-run totals for I/O and processes started have no kernel source without root (io delegation needs a system drop-in: fixed rule 2). A builder who reads pids.peak as processes reports threads; one who reports I/O from the group reports nothing. Attribution of I/O for tagged runs on Linux fails, and docs/09's 'Full' would be shown by doctor.
findings.proposed_change: docs/09-telemetry.md row 1, Linux: 'cpu.stat, memory.* and pids.* (pids count threads); no io.stat and no started-process count without root'; Without admin: 'Partial on Linux'. docs/17-build-prompt.md:62 add: 'On Linux the kernel gives CPU time and memory only. Processes started is unavailable for a tagged run (never pids.peak); I/O comes from the source chosen below, labelled with its gap, or is shown as unavailable.' docs/05-data-flow.md:52: 'CPU and memory, and on Windows I/O and processes started'.
findings.cost: Three sentences across three documents, plus the owner's choice below.
findings.decision_question: Where should tagged-run I/O come from on Linux? (a) After waiting for the command, the launcher reads its own /proc/self/io: reaped children's I/O folds into the reaper (a-linux/io_children.out.txt 2: '+32.0 MB' through an intermediate shell). Gaps: processes still running when the command returns, and double-forked orphans, which the user's systemd adopts (cgroup_totals 4: parent 'named systemd'), so the value must be labelled partial. (b) As (a), with the holder made a child subreaper (PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER) so orphans come back to it: complete, but it changes which process adopts the tree's orphans, which risks fixed rule 1; not probed. (c) Show tagged I/O on Linux as unavailable. Recommendation: (a) labelled partial, with doctor stating the gap; (c) if a partial label is judged too close to an estimate.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/17:62,117,127, docs/05:52, docs/09:9; the 'where delegated' hedge in docs/09 does not rescue the 'Full' cell or the unhedged docs/17 and docs/05 sentences. Re-checked read-only: io is not passed down below the root, no file in a delegated group counts forks, pids files listed. Re-fetched the kernel doc (TIDs quote present) and the Microsoft page (TotalProcesses quote present, so the gap is Linux-only). Did not re-run cgroup_totals.py or io_children.py (CPU burn and disk writes during others' timing). Changed the lead's 'processes started shown as a lower bound' to 'unavailable', because AGENTS.md forbids showing an estimate under a metric's name, and widened option (a)'s stated gap to include background processes left running and orphans adopted by systemd, not only double-forks.

findings.title: A tagged group's kernel memory figure (memory.current/memory.peak) includes page cache and kernel memory, a different unit from the PSS/USS used for every other workload
findings.evidence: a-linux/cgroup_totals.out.txt 5: child wrote 64 MB and exited: 'the child's own peak resident memory: 16.6 MB', 'memory.current ... after 66.3 MB, memory.peak 70.2 MB, populated 0', 'memory.stat: anon 0.0 MB, file 64.0 MB'. verify-4 probe on this user's 68 live leaf groups: memory.current 9.31 GB, shares anon 0.60, file 0.31, kernel 0.08. a-linux/smaps_cost.out.txt 3: PSS vs memory.current 1.88 vs 2.34, 1.41 vs 1.75, 0.47 vs 0.88 GB (+24% to +87%); anon is close to USS (1.69 vs 1.67, 1.20 vs 1.23, 0.26 vs 0.33). Kernel doc (re-fetched) lists tracked memory as 'Userland memory - page cache and anonymous memory'. Brief: docs/17-build-prompt.md:81 and docs/06-storage.md:83 'USS or PSS'; nothing names the group field.
findings.impact: A tagged build that writes artifacts reports peak memory near its write volume (70 MB for a 17 MB process), and the cache stays charged to an empty group. Tagged and polled workloads are compared in different units (24-87% apart here), and run-over-run peak memory diffs (docs/17:127) track file writes rather than memory.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:81 add: 'For a tagged group on Linux, the figure comparable with USS is memory.stat anon plus memory.swap.current, sampled by the collector. memory.current and memory.peak include page cache and kernel memory: store the peak labelled "charged memory, includes file cache" and never add it to PSS or USS.' docs/06-storage.md:83: note the Linux tagged unit.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/17:81, docs/06:83, docs/09:9: no group memory field is named, so not handled; R06 is about leak detection under trimming, not this. Re-checked read-only on live groups with my own probe: 31% of this user's charged group memory is file cache and 8% kernel, so the unit difference holds without the lead's write test. Did not repeat the 64 MB write. Kept medium: the figure is misleading, not invented. Not checked: what a Windows Job's peak memory measures (committed memory per Microsoft's naming), which would make the two platforms differ again.

findings.title: The built-in serious 'memory nearly full' alert and the Memory commit tile read about 265% on a Linux desktop under default overcommit, so the alert fires after two minutes and never clears
findings.evidence: verify-4 probe now: 'vm.overcommit_memory 0; Committed_AS / CommitLimit 2.65'; memory in use 0.62; 'the built-in rule commit_fraction above 0.90 would be: True' (lead: 2.74 and 2.64). https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/proc.html (re-fetched), CommitLimit: 'This limit is only adhered to if strict overcommit accounting is enabled (mode 2 in vm.overcommit_memory).' Brief: docs/08-configuration.md:138 'commit_fraction | machine | Memory commit as a share of the commit limit'; :148 'memory nearly full | machine | commit_fraction | above 0.90 | 2m | serious', switched on by default; docs/17-build-prompt.md:83 and :182 list commit with no platform split; docs/02-what-it-looks-like.md:31 'Memory commit' tile; docs/13-build-list.md:16 providers.system collects commit. Only docs/07-analysis.md:97 (verdict) and docs/09:20 split commit by platform.
findings.impact: On Linux with the default heuristic overcommit, the default serious alert fires two minutes after start and stays on, with a desktop notification every cooldown, and the commit tile shows over 100%. The live-diagnosis job is noisy from the first minute.
findings.proposed_change: docs/08-configuration.md:138: 'commit_fraction: Windows; on Linux only when vm.overcommit_memory = 2, otherwise unavailable'. :148 and docs/17:182: on Linux the built-in rule uses memory pressure (PSI memory full) instead. docs/02-what-it-looks-like.md:31: the Linux tile shows memory in use (1 - MemAvailable/MemTotal).
findings.cost: Three table cells and one clause.
findings.verification: Re-read every cited line; docs/07 verdict and docs/09:20 split by platform, but the metric list, built-in rule, tile and build list do not, and the metric is deliverable on Linux (so the 'unavailable' rule would not stop a builder computing it). Re-read /proc/meminfo with my own probe (2.65, mode 0) and re-fetched the kernel doc: the quoted sentence is present and says CommitLimit is not enforced in modes 0 and 1. The exact ratio depends on swap size and workload, so 'on a normal desktop' means 'commonly', not always; severity kept high because a default-on serious alert is permanently wrong whenever it happens.

findings.title: Linux cannot stop a tagged tree leaving its group: descendants started through systemd-run or snap launchers, and a nested 'submeter run' that asks systemd for a new scope, drop out of the outer run's kernel total
findings.evidence: a-linux/cgroup_leaving.out.txt 2: 'a plain child: still inside the group'; 'through systemd-run --user --scope: OUTSIDE the group'; 'through the launcher of a snap (firefox): OUTSIDE the group' (the probe uses 'snap run --shell', cgroup_leaving.py:115, it did not start the app). cgroup_totals 7: 'a tagged process moving itself to a sibling group: ended up in away; CPU time charged to the group it left: 0.002 s'. cgroup_totals 6: a nested group's usage counts in its parent and stays after removal. Kernel doc (re-fetched): 'The writer must have write access to the cgroup.procs file of the common ancestor of the source and destination cgroups.' (the whole user@N.service subtree is user-owned, verify-4 probe). Brief: docs/17-build-prompt.md:62 'nested jobs' (Windows), :69 'Do not allow breakaway'.
findings.impact: 'Do not allow breakaway' has no Linux equivalent. Descendants started through systemd-run, snap or flatpak launchers run elsewhere and the run file's 'authoritative' kernel total omits them; polling still attributes them through ppid, but only at polled precision, and cost/diff read the run total. A tagged agent that runs 'submeter run --as builds -- pytest' loses the build from its own total under a new-scope design, while on Windows nested jobs keep it.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:69, Linux sentence: 'Linux cannot forbid leaving the group; polling still attributes such a process through its parent, and the run file says the kernel total excludes it. A launcher that finds itself in a tagged group nests by making a sibling of payload/main inside the outer payload and moving itself there, so the inner run counts in the outer one.' docs/10-known-limits.md: a row for descendants started through systemd-run, snap or flatpak launchers.
findings.cost: Two sentences and one table row.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/17:62,69 and docs/10. Narrowed the finding: D-Bus activation, which the lead lists, is already covered by docs/10-known-limits.md:9 ('anything started through a service is charged to itself', R21), so only the run's own descendants that move themselves and nested runs remain. Read cgroup_leaving.py to confirm what it launched. Did not re-run it (it creates scopes during others' timing). The containment rule is in the re-fetched kernel doc. Kept medium, not critical: the escaped processes stay attributed through ppid, so the workload series is preserved and only the run total understates. Replaced the lead's 'sub-group of its own payload group, CPU time only' with the payload/main layout from L2, which keeps memory and pids for nested runs; that layout follows the probe's rules (cgroup_totals 6) but was not run end to end.

findings.title: Per-process GPU load on Linux is not 'NVML or AMD sysfs, Full': amdgpu sysfs is device-wide, Intel has no source in the brief, and the per-process DRM fdinfo source is own-user only
findings.evidence: verify-4 probe: cards {card1 i915, card2-5 evdi}, no gpu_busy_percent file; 12 processes with a DRM client in fdinfo; other users' processes 'fdinfo denied 294, readable 0'. https://docs.kernel.org/gpu/amdgpu/thermal.html (re-fetched): 'The SMU firmware computes a percentage of load based on the aggregate activity level in the IP cores.'; no per-process file on the page. https://docs.kernel.org/gpu/drm-usage-stats.html (re-fetched): 'One purpose of this output is to enable writing as generic as practically feasible top(1) like userspace monitoring tools.'; 'drm-engine-<keystr>: <uint> ns'; driver sections list i915, Xe, Panfrost, Panthor, Amdxdna. Brief: docs/09-telemetry.md:13 'NVML for NVIDIA, sysfs for AMD | Full'; docs/07-analysis.md:100 (not :99) Linux GPU-bound 'NVML utilisation above 90%'; docs/17-build-prompt.md:87 'On Linux use NVML and sysfs.'
findings.impact: On Intel and AMD Linux machines a builder following the brief delivers no per-process GPU load and no Linux GPU-bound verdict, while doctor reports 'Full'. Other users' GPU clients are invisible in any case.
findings.proposed_change: docs/09-telemetry.md:13, Linux: 'NVML for NVIDIA; DRM fdinfo drm-engine-* per process where the driver provides it (i915 and xe documented); amdgpu gpu_busy_percent for device load only'; Without admin: 'Own user only'. docs/07-analysis.md:100 and docs/17:87 to match: 'busiest DRM engine or NVML utilisation above 90%'.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/09:13, docs/07:100 (lead cited :99), docs/17:87; R14 covers engine percentages not adding, not the Linux source. Re-ran the read-only part with my own probe (same cards, same 12 clients, other users' fdinfo all denied). Re-fetched both kernel pages: quotes present. One correction: the drm-usage-stats page does not list amdgpu among its driver sections (it says the deprecated drm-memory key 'is only printed by amdgpu'), so the proposal names only i915 and xe as documented instead of 'i915, xe, amdgpu'. NVML's per-process figure was not tested (no NVIDIA card), so that half of the row is unchanged.

findings.title: With the defaults, the PSS/USS reading costs about 0.7-0.8% of a core on Linux, and with the measured /proc read it puts the collector over the 1% idle budget on a desktop with about 8 GB in its largest processes
findings.evidence: a-linux/smaps_cost.out.txt 1 (reader CPU time, not wall): 'smaps_rollup 24,570 us (29.3 ms per GB)', '25.1 ms per GB'; 'smaps_rollup for the 25 largest: 241.6 ms a round, which at one round every 30 s is 0.805% of a core'. psutil 7.2.2 uses the same file: .venv .../psutil/_pslinux.py:1940-1942 'if HAS_PROC_SMAPS_ROLLUP: ... self._parse_smaps_rollup()'. verify-4 probe, arithmetic only: own top 25 hold 8.23 GB now; at 25.1-29.3 ms per GB every 30 s: 0.69-0.80% of a core; 241.6/30000 = 0.805%. probes/measure/snapshot_cost.out.txt:14: direct /proc stat+statm+io '0.5% at 5 s' (449 processes). Defaults docs/08-configuration.md:66-67 (uss_interval 30s, uss_top_n 25; ranges allow 10s and 200); budget docs/17-build-prompt.md:230 and R02.
findings.impact: The slow memory reading alone takes 70-80% of the 1% idle budget here; with the measured per-tick /proc read (0.3-0.5% at 5 s) the total is about 1.1-1.3%, over budget. The cost scales with resident size, so larger machines exceed it further. The guard (docs/17:191) then slows cadence, so the budget holds by coarser data; the phase 1 CI soak, on runners with little resident memory, would not show it.
findings.proposed_change: docs/08-configuration.md:66-67: 'On Linux the reading costs about 25-30 ms of CPU per GB resident in the processes read; with the defaults that is about 0.8% of a core on a desktop with 8 GB in its 25 largest processes. The overhead guard stretches uss_interval or shrinks uss_top_n before it slows the hot set.' docs/17-build-prompt.md:230: phase 0 measures one USS round as well as one sample. For tagged groups, take memory from memory.stat (see L4) rather than smaps.
findings.verification: Did not re-time (instruction). Checked the arithmetic (241.6 ms / 30 s = 0.805%), recomputed the top-25 resident size read-only (8.23 GB, so 0.69-0.80% at the lead's own rates), and confirmed psutil's fallback reads smaps_rollup, so the measured file is the one any build would read. Added the shared measurement from probes/measure/snapshot_cost.out.txt to show the combined total crosses the idle budget. The baseline provider does not read USS yet (psutil_provider.py has no memory_full_info call), so this is a design default, not a code defect. Kept medium: the guard keeps the budget by degrading cadence, so no job fails outright. R02 mentions USS cost growing with memory but gives no figure and no guard order.

findings.title: On Linux other users' command lines are readable, and the baseline reads, matches rules on and stores them, though the brief says they are not readable
findings.evidence: verify-4 probe: /proc options 'rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime', hidepid set False; other users' processes with a non-empty command line 134, with arguments 67; 'baseline provider: 452 processes; other users' (root included) handed on with a command line: 134'. Code: src/submeter/providers/psutil_provider.py:67-71 reads cmdline for every process; src/submeter/attribution/rules.py:149-156 tries rules (including command-line patterns) before the Restricted bucket; src/submeter/store/raw.py:153-157 stores the redacted text. Brief: docs/10-known-limits.md:16 'Command lines and USS are not readable'; docs/02-what-it-looks-like.md:150-153 '14 processes owned by other users ... Command lines and USS are not readable, because Submeter never runs elevated.' Kernel proc doc (re-fetched): 'hidepid=invisible or hidepid=2 means hidepid=1 plus all /proc/<pid>/ will be fully invisible to other users.'
findings.impact: On a shared Linux machine Submeter stores other accounts' and root's arguments (secrets the scrub misses included) for 48 hours, contrary to the stated behaviour; nothing leaves the machine, so fixed rule 3 holds. Command-line rules match other users' processes on Linux, so rules.toml behaves differently from the stated design. With hidepid=2 the opposite happens: those processes vanish from /proc and from Restricted, which the brief also does not cover.
findings.proposed_change: Either way: docs/10-known-limits.md:16 and docs/02-what-it-looks-like.md:152 get Linux wording ('CPU time, memory, name and command line are readable; I/O, USS, working folder and executable path are not'), and doctor reports hidepid from the /proc mount options. If (a) is chosen: psutil_provider.py and the phase-1 /proc reader leave cmdline as None when the process's real uid differs from the collector's, with a test, and docs/17 Privacy says 'Submeter keeps only the name of another user's process.'
findings.cost: Two text cells, one sentence, and about five lines of provider code plus a test.
findings.decision_question: Other users' command lines on Linux: (a) do not keep them (name only), so the store holds no other account's arguments and command-line rules behave as the brief describes; (b) keep reading them, redacted, and correct the two documents to say Linux shows them. Recommendation: (a). The brief's privacy section exists because command lines carry secrets, and the readable set here includes root's. It costs only command-line rules aimed at other users' processes, which the brief never promised.
findings.verification: Re-read psutil_provider.py:54-101, rules.py:135-160, raw.py:150-160 and both brief passages. Re-ran the counts with my own read-only probe (counts only, no command line saved): 134 readable and 67 with arguments, matching the lead; the baseline provider hands all 134 on. Re-fetched the hidepid quote. R04 redacts secrets but does not limit whose command lines are kept, so it does not cover this. Merged the two leads; severity set between them (A: medium, D: low) at medium, because two brief passages state something false on Linux and attribution behaves differently from them. Made it needs_decision, because the lead's code change drops information the rules currently use, and the brief statement is a capability claim, not a stated policy. The hidepid=2 case (processes missing from Restricted and from reconciliation) is a second issue, quoted from the kernel doc but not tested here (no hidepid on this machine). Windows behaviour for other users' command lines was not verified.
